method: Read ch.4 'Routine' (the four cycles and seasonal routines) and ch.6 'Pathology' in full (epub, no fixed page numbers; cited by chapter and section heading). This is Svoboda's second book in Nimai's knowledge base (the first, Prakriti, already sources the dosha-temperament content). Ch.6's six-stage disease model is the classical reason the app's Vikriti check exists; ch.4's day, season and age cycles corroborate the Govardhan workbook's 'increased by' timings and translate its Indian-calendar seasons for temperate climates. Together they stand in for Lad's Ayurveda: The Science of Self-Healing, which was never available.

claims.paraphrase: Every illness, whatever the underlying dosha, is described as following the same six-stage progression: Accumulation, Aggravation, Overflow, Location, Manifestation and Specialization. The first three stages happen before a dosha has settled anywhere specific in the body; only from Location onward does a recognizable illness begin to take shape.

At the accumulation stage, a dosha has simply built up in its home organ — kapha in the stomach, pitta in the small intestine, vata in the colon — each producing its own mild, early symptoms (kapha: heaviness and dulled appetite; pitta: burning and irritability; vata: dryness, disturbed sleep, mild anxiety). The text is explicit that the doshas are easiest to correct at this stage, before they've gone anywhere or caused a specific illness, and that routine seasonal care is what normally clears this kind of accumulation before it can progress.

If accumulation isn't addressed, the dosha intensifies where it sits (aggravation) — still fairly straightforward to treat at this stage, though by now the organ under pressure needs support too, not just the dosha itself.

Only once a dosha has left its home organ, circulated, and settled somewhere already weakened does a specific illness begin to take shape — this stage is marked by 'premonitory symptoms', early warning signs specific to whatever is about to develop, which appear before the condition is fully recognizable or diagnosable.

The text names weak digestive fire as the root cause of disease in general, vata as the chief driver of how diseases develop and spread, and ama (the residue of incompletely digested food) as disease's principal nourishment — a framing that puts routine digestive care ahead of treating any single symptom.

Across the day, kapha predominates from dawn to mid-morning, pitta from mid-morning to mid-afternoon, and vata from mid-afternoon to dusk. The night repeats the pattern: kapha for roughly the first third after dusk, pitta through the midnight hours, and vata in the hours before dawn. Vata as a whole is strongest at the junctions of day and night.

claims.pages: ch.4, Routine (The seasons of the year)
claims.paraphrase: Classical texts describe six Indian seasons, but for most temperate countries the pattern is: kapha builds up in winter and is aggravated in spring; pitta builds up in spring and is aggravated in summer; vata builds up in summer and predominates in autumn, settling again in winter unless the cold is extreme.

Kapha predominates strongly until about sixteen and remains dominant until about thirty; pitta predominates through middle age; vata predominates after about sixty, as the body dries and people feel the cold more.

Ayurveda holds that illness tends to arise at the junctions of cycles - the change from one season to the next, dawn and dusk, adolescence and menopause - because every adaptation a system has to make raises the chance of imbalance. Regular seasonal care at those junctions is the traditional protection.
